title: Development charges study approved after public meeting
subtitle: Parkland purchase on Lexington Road, dangerous dogs by-law, conservation authority consolidation, drinking water report and nuisance rules.
overview: Council approved the 2026 Development Charges Background Study after a formal public meeting {{vote:m10}}. These charges are fees on new development that pay for growth-related infrastructure and facilities, including parks, recreation, water, roads and sewers. Staff said the by-law setting the new rates would come back for adoption in about a month.

Council released $1,334,000 in capital funding to buy 279 Lexington Road, which will enlarge an existing city park {{vote:m7}}. It replaced the Dangerous Dog By-law with an updated version {{vote:m8}} and approved updated penalty wording {{vote:m9}} and Nuisance By-law amendments {{vote:m4}}. Council also approved Traffic and Parking By-law amendments, received a residential speed management update, and approved the 2025 drinking water reports {{vote:m6}}.

Council asked the province to consult municipalities before consolidating Ontario's conservation authorities {{vote:m11}}. A resident also asked council to consider a pilot program for backyard wood fires. No motion followed, so the open-air fire rules are unchanged.

decisions.detail: Council approved the 2026 Development Charges Background Study and report CORP2026-003 following the formal public meeting.
Council released $1,334,000 in 2026 parkland acquisition funding and authorized the Mayor and Clerk to sign the purchase agreement.
Council repealed and replaced the 1998 Dangerous Dog By-law and amended the Screening and Hearing Officer By-law and administrative penalty schedule.
Council asked the province to consult municipalities and the Grand River Conservation Authority on the proposed consolidation and sent the motion to provincial and municipal bodies.
Council approved amendments to the Nuisance By-law 2011-125 under report COM2026-007.
Council received the 2025 annual and summary drinking water reports required under provincial regulation and approved report IPPW2026-004.

debate: A resident asked for a time-limited pilot for regulated backyard fires, arguing that permits, setbacks and seasonal bans could address safety and enforcement concerns. Councillors thanked the delegate and noted the current rules allow gas-fuelled fires. Council took no action.

One development charges delegate supported the study, arguing that charges are a small share of home prices and fund services that residents value. They also backed keeping the West Side Recreation Facility on schedule.

A real estate association delegate opposed increases, arguing that higher charges are passed on to buyers and reduce affordability. Neighbouring cities have cut or paused charges. Councillors asked how price reductions would be tracked, and the delegate said they would follow up.

Councillors supporting the development charges study said it is a ten-year plan. They said it funds infrastructure capacity for planned growth and that Waterloo remains below Kitchener and Cambridge. Staff noted that discretionary exemptions must be funded from other sources such as property taxes.
On conservation authorities, councillors said municipalities fund these bodies and should be consulted. They also raised the importance of local watershed knowledge for regional drinking water.
